passage:
I'm Tenzin, and I supervise the second-year students in Dr Bose's lab. For three months Nirmala has been my easiest student. Extra data runs? "Yes, Tenzin, I'll do it." The outreach workshop, the poster, the department fest committee: yes, yes, yes. Each time I wrote "Excellent work!" on her reports, and each time she stood a little taller.
Last Friday I came in at seven and found her asleep over the bench, cheek on her notebook, a half-eaten biscuit beside her. She jolted up, laughing. "Just resting my eyes!"
I can't know what she's feeling. Most days she looks proud and lit up. But it struck me that every bit of praise I've given her has been about output. I've never once asked whether she still sings with the college choir, or when she last took a Sunday off.
This week I'm going to try asking.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin find Nirmala at seven last Friday?
qa.a: Asleep over the bench, cheek on her notebook, with a half-eaten biscuit beside her.

qa.q: What might Nirmala have been feeling when she jolted up laughing, 'Just resting my eyes!'?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed to be caught asleep and wanted to keep looking like the tireless student, though Tenzin can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Tenzin notice or praise from now on?
qa.a: Tenzin could ask about the choir and days off, and praise Nirmala for resting or turning something down, not only for results.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nirmala to hear only 'Excellent work!'?
qa.a: Nirmala may feel valued mostly when producing more, so saying yes keeps the praise coming even as her sleep runs short.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing a proud student who says yes to everything and realising that praising only output has fed the overload.

passage:
Monday. Leela burst in waving her phone: elected class representative, picked for the college dance team, and a café wanting her to design their menu, paid. Her mother, Seema, hugged her. "That's my girl! Is there anything you can't do?" Leela beamed all through dinner.
Thursday, two weeks later. Seema woke at midnight to find Leela eating cold dal standing at the counter, laptop open to the menu. "Skipped dance," Leela said. "The rep meeting ran late." Her marks sheet lay on the table, all A grades. Seema began to say "Wonderful," then stopped. When had she last heard Leela laugh?
Sunday. Over tea, Seema tried a new question. "What did you actually enjoy this week?" Leela thought for a long time. "Nothing, really. Dance, maybe, when I went."
"Then maybe dance stays and something else goes. And I'm proud you slept till ten today."
Leela rolled her eyes, but she smiled.

qa.q: What three things did Leela announce on Monday?
qa.a: She was elected class representative, picked for the college dance team, and a café wanted her to design their menu, paid.

qa.q: Why did Seema stop herself from saying 'Wonderful' about the marks?
qa.a: Finding Leela eating cold dal at midnight worried her; she realised she couldn't remember Leela's last laugh, so praising marks suddenly felt wrong.

qa.q: Which of Seema's two responses helps more at this stage, and why?
qa.a: The Sunday one, asking what Leela enjoyed and praising her for sleeping in, because it values rest, limits and enjoyment rather than only results.

qa.q: What might Leela be feeling when her mother asks what she enjoyed?
qa.a: Leela may be caught off guard, noticing for the first time that almost nothing felt good that week, and a little relieved to be praised for resting.

grounding: Illustrates a parent who first praises a daughter's growing list of achievements, then notices the missing rest and joy and changes what she praises.

The clinic waiting room at the tech park smelled of sanitiser, and Gopika's head was pounding for the third time that week. Arnab sat beside her, scrolling nothing.
Last night she had snapped at him over a wet towel, then locked herself in the bathroom, stomach churning, while the Sunday-night dread about Monday's release crept in.
"I'm just weak," she muttered. "Other engineers manage twelve-hour days."
Arnab didn't argue. "You never used to shout about towels."
Inside, the doctor asked about sleep, meals and work hours before anything else. Gopika listed them and heard herself: in by eight, logging off after midnight, lunch at her desk if at all.
The doctor made a few notes. "Let's check a few things. And let's also talk about that schedule."
On the way out, Gopika looked at the hours written in her own handwriting and felt a small, cold jolt of fear.

qa.q: What did Gopika snap at Arnab about last night?
qa.a: She snapped at him over a wet towel.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel when she looked at her hours written down, and why?
qa.a: She felt a small, cold jolt of fear, because the hours suggested the schedule, not weakness, might be behind the headaches and churning stomach 😰.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Gopika now?
qa.a: She can follow up with the doctor and treat the headaches, stomach trouble and temper as a message to change the hours, rather than proof that she is weak.

qa.q: What is Arnab experiencing as he sits beside her?
qa.a: Arnab has been on the receiving end of her temper and sees she has changed; he stays close and quietly points out that this isn't who she used to be.

Dhruv,
It's Sunday, 10:40 pm, and I'm writing this instead of sleeping because my stomach has been in a knot since about four. It's like this every Sunday now. Just thinking of the 9 am stand-up makes my chest go tight.
I've had a headache most days this month. Last week I shouted at Maa because she asked if I'd eaten. She only asked! I apologised, but I could see she was hurt.
I keep telling myself I'm just not tough enough for this job. But you know me. I survived hostel, I survived final year. I wasn't like this six months ago, before we got the second project and the weekend calls started.
Maybe it isn't me that's broken. Maybe it's the schedule.
Writing that down feels scary, and a bit like relief.
Tell me honestly if I sound ridiculous.
Yogesh

qa.a: The 9 am stand-up.

qa.q: Why does writing 'Maybe it's the schedule' feel scary and a bit like relief to Yogesh?
qa.a: It means admitting the job's load is the problem, which is frightening, but it also loosens the belief that Yogesh is simply not tough enough.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do next with what the body is signalling?
qa.a: Yogesh could see a doctor about the daily headaches and stomach knots, and raise the second project and weekend calls with the manager rather than pushing through.

qa.a: Maa had only asked about eating, so she was hurt, and she may be worried about how changed her child seems.

grounding: Illustrates a young engineer's headaches, stomach knots, snapping at home and Sunday dread as signals that the workload is the problem.

Deadline day, and the open-plan floor was loud with printers and ringing phones. Tanvir noticed that Damini had skipped lunch again; her tiffin was still zipped at four o'clock. She used to bring laddoos for everyone's birthdays. This week she had snapped at the intern, forgotten a client's name mid-call and sent the same file twice.
In the team huddle, Varun joked, "Who stole our Damini's smile?" Everyone laughed. Damini didn't.
Tanvir waited until she went to refill her bottle, then followed her to the quiet pantry. "Hey. Just us, not in front of everyone. You've seemed really worn out lately. How are you actually doing?"
Damini stared at the tap. "Headaches every day. I can't sleep."
"That sounds rough. Would you see a doctor about the headaches and the sleep this week? I can cover your Thursday call."
She let out a long breath and nodded.

qa.q: What did Damini used to bring to the office?
qa.a: She used to bring laddoos for everyone's birthdays.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt when Varun joked in the huddle?
qa.a: She probably felt exposed and more worn down; she didn't laugh when everyone else did.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir's approach work better than the huddle joke?
qa.a: Tanvir spoke privately in the quiet pantry, named the change gently, suggested a doctor for the headaches and sleep, and offered to cover a call instead of making a public remark.

qa.q: What was the difference for Damini between the huddle and the pantry?
qa.a: In the huddle her change became a joke in front of everyone; in the pantry she felt safe enough to admit daily headaches and poor sleep.

passage:
In the small insurance office above a sweet shop in Lajpat Nagar, Vikas used to be the one who hummed old film songs while filing claims. Lately Sunaina heard only his stapler, slammed. He forgot the Monday review, barked at the office boy over cold tea, and his lunch box went home full three days running.
On Wednesday, in front of the whole team, she tried to lighten things. "Vikas, just take a holiday, yaar!" He went red and said nothing for the rest of the day.
That evening she walked out with him towards the metro. "Sorry about earlier. That wasn't the place. You don't seem yourself, and I'm a bit worried."
Vikas kicked a pebble. "Stomach's been bad for weeks. I'm not sleeping."
"Would you show a doctor? Not a holiday. A doctor first. I'll come along if you want."
Near the metro gate, he finally nodded.

qa.q: What did Vikas used to do while filing claims?
qa.a: He used to hum old film songs.

qa.q: Why might Vikas have gone red and stayed silent after Sunaina's remark?
qa.a: Being told to take a holiday in front of the whole team probably embarrassed him and made his struggle feel both exposed and brushed aside.

qa.q: How did Sunaina repair her first mistake?
qa.a: She apologised, spoke privately on the walk to the metro, said she was worried, and suggested a doctor rather than just a holiday, offering to go along.

qa.q: What was the walk to the metro like for Vikas compared with the team meeting?
qa.a: Away from the team, Vikas felt safe enough to admit weeks of stomach trouble and poor sleep, and the offer of company made a doctor's visit feel less daunting.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague whose public 'take a holiday' remark backfires, followed by a private check-in that points a sharp, forgetful teammate to a doctor.

passage:
The plotter jammed at 6:10 pm, twenty minutes before the municipal submission, and Swati simply sat down on the print-room floor of the architecture firm.
She didn't decide to cry. It just came, heavy and shaking, the kind she couldn't stop by breathing.
Yogesh, her team lead, found her there. He crouched a little distance away. "I'll email the drawings myself. You're going home."
"I can do it," she said, and couldn't even stand.
In the cab she stared at her hands. Three years without missing a deadline, and now this. Pathetic, she thought.
At home she slept fourteen hours without waking. The next morning her body felt like wet sand.
Yogesh had messaged: "Submission went through. Take tomorrow off. Let's talk on Thursday about your load, no pressure."
She read it twice and felt ashamed and, underneath that, strangely grateful.

qa.q: How long did Swati sleep after she got home?
qa.a: She slept fourteen hours without waking.

qa.q: What did Swati think of herself in the cab, and why?
qa.a: She thought she was pathetic, because after three years without missing a deadline, breaking down felt like failure.

qa.q: What turning point does Yogesh's message open for Swati?
qa.a: It lets her rest properly and then talk honestly on Thursday about her load, treating the crash as a signal rather than a failure.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt finding Swati on the print-room floor?
qa.a: He may have been shaken to see a reliable team member unable to stand, and chose to take the task off her and send her home instead of pushing the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young professional breaking down before a deadline and sleeping fourteen hours, a crash that feels like failure but is the body forcing rest.

passage:
Thomas,
I'm writing this from bed at 3 pm on a Monday. The quarterly deck was due at ten. I set four alarms. I heard every one of them, and I could not make my body get up. Not lazy-couldn't. Couldn't, like my arms were filled with sand.
At eleven I finally messaged my manager: "Unwell, can't make it today." Then I cried for an hour, because I have never, ever done that.
It feels like I've failed at the one thing I'm known for. You know me, the 2 am edits person.
But lying here I keep thinking how I've been saying "I'll rest after this project" since March. Maybe my body just stopped waiting for me to agree.
I'm scared of what I'll say to my manager tomorrow.
Can you call me tonight?
Noor

qa.q: How many alarms did Noor set?
qa.a: Noor set four alarms.

qa.q: Why does Noor feel like a failure after missing the deadline?
qa.a: Noor is upset because Noor is known for 2 am edits and has never missed work like this, so staying in bed feels like failing at the one thing Noor is known for.

qa.q: What could Noor do before facing the manager tomorrow?
qa.a: Noor could rest today, talk it through with Thomas tonight and plan to be honest about months of overwork; if the heavy tiredness keeps going, a doctor visit would help.

qa.q: What might Thomas feel when this letter arrives?
qa.a: Thomas may be worried to hear that a friend who never misses deadlines couldn't get out of bed, and glad to be the one Noor reached out to.

grounding: Illustrates being unable to get out of bed for a Monday deadline, feeling it as failure while sensing the body has enforced overdue rest.

Farida had rehearsed it in the auto, but in the coordinator's small office at the school her voice still shook.
"Nandini ma'am, I need to be honest. I'm teaching five sections, running the annual day and taking the Saturday remedial class. I've been eating lunch standing up and sleeping about five hours. Last month I cried in the staffroom. I don't want to wait until I can't come in at all."
Nandini put down her pen. "Thank you for telling me now and not in April. Which one can go?"
"The annual day. Mr Kurian offered to help anyway. And I'd like my Saturdays back for two months."
"Done. I'll speak to Kurian today and rotate the Saturday class." She paused. "And lunch at the table, please, not standing."
Farida walked out lighter, went straight to the staffroom and sat down to eat.

qa.q: Which duty did Farida ask to hand off?
qa.a: The annual day, which Mr Kurian had offered to help with anyway.

qa.q: Why did Farida's voice still shake even after rehearsing?
qa.a: She was nervous about admitting she couldn't manage everything and may have worried the coordinator would see it as weakness.

qa.q: What made the conversation work for both of them?
qa.a: Farida named her load, her lost sleep and meals and a specific request, and Nandini thanked her and made adjustments instead of blaming her.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Farida speaking up now rather than later?
qa.a: Nandini is grateful to hear it before April, since handing off the annual day and rotating Saturdays is far easier than losing a teacher to a breakdown.

grounding: Shows a young teacher telling her coordinator the truth about her load and handing off tasks, and a manager who responds with changes, not blame.

Subject: My workload, and a request
Hi Disha,
I'd like to be straight with you before this becomes a bigger problem.
Since the Chennai account moved to our team, I've been covering two clients plus the vendor audits. I've worked until 1 am most nights, skipped dinner more often than not, and last Friday I blanked on the client call. That isn't like me, and I don't want it to become normal.
I'd like to propose:
1. Handing the vendor audits to Rohit, who has asked for audit experience.
2. Keeping my calendar clear after 8 pm, except for real emergencies.
3. A check-in with you in two weeks to see how it's going.
I care about this work, which is exactly why I'm raising it now.
Thanks for hearing me out,
Anand

Reply, forty minutes later: "Thank you for flagging this early, Anand. Yes to all three. Let's also look at whether the Chennai account needs one more person. Disha"

qa.q: Who does Anand suggest should take the vendor audits?
qa.a: Rohit, who has asked for audit experience.

qa.q: Why does Anand write 'I care about this work, which is exactly why I'm raising it now'?
qa.a: Anand wants the email read as commitment rather than complaint, and seems worried it might look like weakness.

qa.q: What in Anand's email makes it easy for a manager to act on?
qa.a: It is honest about the late nights, skipped dinners and the blank on the call, and offers three concrete proposals with a check-in date.

qa.q: How does Disha respond, and what does that suggest about Disha as a manager?
qa.a: Disha replies within forty minutes, thanks Anand for flagging it early and agrees to all three, which suggests a manager who adjusts rather than blames.

grounding: Illustrates telling a manager the truth about workload, handing off a task and protecting evenings, with the manager answering with adjustments.

I'm Chinmay, Eshaan's flatmate, so I've watched the last two months up close, though I can only guess what's going on inside.
After the leave in August, the first weeks were mostly sleep and cricket highlights. Then small changes. A walk to the lake every evening, ten minutes at first, now nearly an hour. Sunday calls to Eshaan's Aai and Baba that last longer than "ho, fine." Badminton with me on Saturdays, played badly, with a lot of laughing. Half days at work since September.
Some evenings Eshaan comes home lit up and cooks. Other days it's the sofa, flat, and just, "It's a grey one," and that's that.
Last week the manager praised a report, and I braced for the old overdrive. Instead: "Nice. Anyway, badminton?"
I don't know if that's peace or tiredness. But it's the first time in a year I've heard work mentioned without a number attached.

qa.a: Ten minutes at first, now nearly an hour.

qa.a: Chinmay has watched up close, braced for the old overdrive, and is quietly relieved to hear work mentioned without a number, while admitting it's only a guess what Eshaan feels inside 🙂.

Week one back. Tejas logged in for four hours instead of ten, as agreed with his manager, and still felt guilty closing the laptop at one. That evening his younger brother Hrithik dragged him to the park for cricket. Tejas dropped two catches and went home flat, wondering if he would ever feel normal again.

Week nine. Six-hour days now. At dinner Hrithik asked, "Did you get a lot done?"
Tejas thought about it. "Some. But I beat you at carrom, and Amma laughed at my joke. That counted too."

At the Sri Rama Navami fair in Chaitanya's village, Lalit anna played the harmonium on the temple steps, fingers flying, and the whole crowd clapped along. Chaitanya, nine, forgot all about his cotton candy.
On the walk home he announced to Ammamma, "From tomorrow I will practise harmonium every single day. Like Lalit anna!"
Ammamma's old harmonium sat under a cloth in the storeroom. Next morning Chaitanya dragged it out before brushing his teeth and pumped the bellows till dust flew. He played the same three notes over and over, grinning. After school he played again. After dinner he played on the veranda until the neighbour's dog howled.
"Every day," he told Ammamma, tapping her arm. "You'll see."

Third week of the monsoon holidays in Bishnupur, and Anirban's tabla practice had gone grey. The first days had been thrilling: new bols, Baba recording him on the old phone, Thakuma clapping from the veranda. Now it was the same teen-taal, round and round, and his fingers still stumbled on the same fast phrase. Ustadji said it would take months.
From the lane came Jeevan's whistle. "Anirban! Fishing at the big pond, everyone's going!"
Anirban looked at the tabla, then at the rain-washed lane. One day off won't matter, he thought. I practised yesterday. I'll do double tomorrow.

qa.a: He could do a short, fixed practice before joining Jeevan, so the habit rests on a simple rule rather than on whether he feels like it.

qa.a: Jeevan probably just wants his friend at the pond and may not realise Anirban is torn between fun and a practice that has gone dull.

Day nineteen of the plan Lars had copied into his notebook: jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening. In week one he'd felt like an athlete. Now, on Bergen's third straight day of rain, he checked his arms in the bathroom mirror and saw exactly the same arms.
His brother Daniel, home from university, glanced up from the sofa. "Going out in that?"
Lars pulled on one shoe and stopped. It's just rain, he told himself. Then another voice: skip today, the plan says rest days are fine anyway. It didn't, actually.
He sat on the bottom stair, one shoe on and the other in his hand, feeling nothing like the boy who had started this. Daniel said nothing, just raised an eyebrow.
Lars tied the second lace slowly, not because he wanted to, but because he'd said he would.

qa.q: What was Lars's evening plan?
qa.a: Jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening.

qa.q: What does Lars's thought 'the plan says rest days are fine anyway' reveal?
qa.a: He feels discouraged and bored, so his mind bargains for a skip, even inventing a rule, because his arms look exactly the same.

qa.q: Why did tying the second lace matter, and what might help on the next rainy day?
qa.a: Lars went because he'd said he would, not because he felt like it; a shorter indoor version for rainy days could make discipline easier when mood is low.

passage:
For five weeks Uma had read the Tamil and English newspapers aloud on the thinnai at six every morning, preparing for the bank exam, while the milkman slowed his cycle to listen.
Then came the Pongal trip to Periyamma's village: three days of kolams, cooking and cousins, and no newspaper at all.
Back home in Tiruvarur, the pile of unread papers sat by the door. Uma walked past it on the first morning. And the second.
"Five weeks of work, and I broke it in three days," she told her older sister Jaya, who was stringing jasmine. "What's the use now? I'll start properly after the exam."
"The exam is in March, Uma."
Uma shrugged, the guilt sitting heavy under the shrug, and went inside. By the end of the week the papers had spread into a small, yellowing hill.

qa.q: Where did Uma read the newspapers every morning?
qa.a: On the thinnai at six every morning.

qa.q: What does Uma's 'What's the use now?' reveal about how she sees the break?
qa.a: She feels guilty and treats three days away as having ruined five weeks, so she thinks the routine may as well stop.

qa.q: What small step could turn this slip around?
qa.a: Uma could read just one paper aloud the next morning, counting the Pongal days as a pause rather than a failure, and let Jaya remind her of the five weeks already done.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel watching the pile of papers grow?
qa.a: Jaya, who gently pointed out that the exam is in March, may be worried to see her sister's hard work slip away over a short festival break.

grounding: Illustrates a festival trip breaking a study routine, followed by guilt and all-or-nothing thinking that turns a short gap into stopping.
